Boellstorff entered SL much as if he were landing on an island, where he initially would depend on a small number of informants who would help him learn to function in their social world. He was clear about his identity as an anthropologist (using the online name Tom Bukowski) as well as his mission, spreading the word that he wanted opportunities to learn about all aspects of the society. Over his time in SL he conducted formal interviews in individual and group formats but he also shopped in local stores, developed a wide variety of personal relationships, visited residents in their homes, and became a valued member of community organizations. He had access to computer-specific tools, including the ability to design his appearance and shape his own living space so that they would help to clarify his identity, and he was able to gather large volumes of text conversation. This approach was ideal for study of a culture that was changing so fast—and was so complex—that its members themselves could not describe the culture of which they were a part. SL is not the first virtual society to be noticed by scholars. The implications of computer-mediated relationships have been explored for decades (e.g., Turkle, 1984). Computer games, in the 1970s and 1980s, developed into online “multiuser dungeons,” where players could pool their resources to create complex environments. Even before the term “virtual” gained its conventional meanings related to the Internet, groups of people established unique sets of relational patterns and cultural meanings meeting in local computer networks. More recently, social networking sites are producing new kinds of virtual relationships. Boellstorff, who uses the term “virtual” in unique ways, suggests that cyber-technology is merely a new version of an inherently human history. For example, he observes that newspapers in earlier generations created communities by connecting physically separated populations in shared networks of meaning. Viewed in this way, SL is not inherently different from the family groupings, cities, religious institutions, political parties, sports teams, universities, and other cultures that have been more typically the focus of academic attention. He claims, “It is in being virtual that we are human” (p. 29). Even if it is not unique in its essential symbolic nature, however, SL seems to offer family scholars a unique opportunity to examine many levels of symbolic exchange interacting in an emerging society. SL residents, in the period of time chronicled by Boellstorff, communicated to a great extent through text, generating a record that could be preserved and examined (he refers to collecting 10,000 pages of transcripts). Users were aware of being cocreators of their unique environment, and they discussed it at length in private as well as public conversations. They critiqued their own virtual world and both celebrated and challenged the ways in which it influenced their identities and relationships. The environment was also being studied and manipulated by the corporate management of Linden Labs, which operates SL as a profit-generating business. Therefore all residents were not equal; mixed into the population were engineers, marketing specialists, and security personnel attempting to limit the negative aspects of SL culture and maximize its appeal to newcomers. Their communication with the rest of the population is part of the record. Coming of Age in Second Life is often mentioned in connection with Donna Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto (1985/1991). Haraway, writing in a time before SL could have been predicted, described her fantasy cyborgs—blurring the boundaries between human and machine—as ironic images that could inspire women to move past binary thinking and imagine their potential free from biological constraints. Neither one thing nor the other, cyborgs could be infinitely varied, embodying the biological and technological elements that best fit the needs of the moment. In recent years this potential is being actualized (Gane, 2006). With help from technology, people are able to augment or replace parts of themselves that do not suit their purposes. Boellstorff finds SL residents saying that their avatars embody some of their real-life characteristics, but they feel more truly themselves when online. He finds many people choosing to change their age, race, gender, or a combination of these, but he also finds individuals with real-world disabilities who speak of their SL experience as an opportunity to live without barriers. Haraway is often cited by those who have speculated, over the past 20 years, on the emergence of a “posthuman” society. Hayles (2006) suggests, for example, that electronic media have transformed life so that the individual person is losing significance when compared with “distributed cultural cognitions.” This portrayal has both optimistic and pessimistic potentials; Hayles expresses hope that relational and distributed agency may improve the species by overcoming the effects of uncontrolled free will. Boellstorff, however, expresses doubts about the term “posthuman” and its portrayal of humans and technology as merging. Technology, he says, is not a recent arrival but is, in fact, the central feature of humanity, both a tool and a product of human effort. The printing press changed human existence, but we remain human, and new forms of techne bring out new aspects of human potential. Tom Boellstorff has created a thoughtful and engaging, thorough picture of SL and its residents. In the process, he continually steps back to question the contributions of scholarship in the larger project of human existence. This award-winning book is rapidly becoming a cornerstone of a growing body of virtual reality literature and, if current trends continue, Coming of Age in Second Life is likely to earn a place on required reading lists for human development and family studies courses.

articles.title: Consequential Strangers and Peripheral Ties: The Importance of Unimportant Relationships
articles.abstract: Social networks in the 21st century include a wide array of partners. Most individuals report a few core ties (primarily family) and hundreds of peripheral ties. Weak ties differ from intimate ties in emotional quality, stability, density (i.e., who knows whom), and status hierarchies. Undoubtedly, close ties are essential for human survival. Yet peripheral ties may enhance life quality and allow people to flourish. Weak ties may serve (a) distinct functions from intimate ties (e.g., information, resources, novel behaviors, and diversion), (b) parallel functions to intimate ties (e.g., defining identity and positions within social hierarchies, helping when a family member is ill, providing a sense of familiarity), and (c) reciprocal influences between peripheral partners and family members (e.g., bioecological theory). Family science might benefit from investigating consequential strangers who pepper daily life.

articles.title: Critical Theorizing: Enhancing Theoretical Rigor in Family Research
articles.abstract: Theory performs vital descriptive, sensitizing, integrative, explanatory, and value functions in the generation of knowledge about families. Yet theory and research can also simultaneously misconceive, desensitize, misdirect, misinterpret, and devalue. Overcoming the degenerative potentialities of theory and research requires attention to critical theorizing, a joint process of (a) critically examining the explicit and implicit assumptions of theory and research and (b) using dialogical theoretical practices. I draw upon the work of John Stuart Mill to argue that critical and dialogical theorizing is a vital and necessary practice in the production of understandings of family phenomena that are more fully scientific and empirical. A brief examination of behavioral research on marital interaction illustrates the importance of critical theorizing.

articles.title: Critiquing the General Theory of Crime's Empirical Evidence: Does the Evidence Support the Theory?
articles.authors: Crosswhite, Jennifer M.; Kerpelman, Jennifer L.
articles.abstract: Gottfredson and Hirschi's general theory of crime proposes that low self‐control leads to engagement in deviant behaviors, parents must properly socialize self‐control in their children, and self‐control fully mediates the parenting‐deviance association. A critical analysis of the empirical evidence generated suggests a number of unresolved issues regarding the theory that remain to be investigated. Some of the specific issues addressed include determining which aspects of parenting influence the etiology of self‐control and to what extent self‐control mediates the parenting‐deviance association.

articles.title: Cultural Theory: Classical and Contemporary Positions.
Disparities in School Readiness: How Families Contribute to Transitions Into School.
Everyday Family Life: Dimensions, Approaches, and Current Challenges
articles.abstract: The aim of this systematic literature review was to identify, categorize, and evaluate the empirical research that has been conducted on everyday family life. Fifty‐three empirically based articles focusing on everyday family life were included in the analysis, which focused on the conceptual, empirical, and theoretical content. According to our review, everyday family life comprises three dimensions: emotions, actions, and temporality. It is a continuously constructed process in which family members transmit emotions, engage in activities, and schedule timetables in the course of interactions with each other and with the wider social context. Three empirical or theoretical approaches were identified: the emotion transmission approach, the cultural activity approach, and the constructionist approach, all of which adopt research methods and concepts sensitive to daily fluctuations.

Institutionalization of the Family and Marriage: Questioning Their Cognitive and Relational Realities
articles.abstract: This paper argues that to explain the institutionalization processes named the family and marriage, it is necessary to recognize the ontological distinction between their cognitive and relational realities. Institutionalization is an ordering process analogous to instinct in animal societies. In that capacity the human family and marriage collectively order the care and social placement of offspring. Given the biology of Homo sapiens, the family preceded the onset of the human race by millions of years, whereas marriage, the contract that legitimates the social placement of offspring, represents a strictly cultural aspect of human social evolution. The current state and uncertain future of the cognitive and relational components of the institutions of the family and marriage are addressed.

articles.title: Keyword Index
Leaving an Abusive Partner: Exploring Boundary Ambiguity Using the Stages of Change Model
articles.authors: Khaw, Lyndal Bee Lian; Hardesty, Jennifer L.
articles.abstract: The Stages of Change Model has helped researchers and practitioners explore the process of leaving an abusive partner, but it does not account for the changes in relational boundaries unique to this process. In this paper, we integrate the concept of boundary ambiguity into the Stages of Change Model to explore potential sources of boundary ambiguity in the process of leaving. We theorize that Boss’s two types of boundary ambiguity may be present at different points of the leaving process and are perceptual barriers to leaving permanently. We also theorize that potential sources of boundary ambiguity emerge from women and their partners’ decisions and actions in the process of leaving. Implications and future directions for research and practice are discussed.

articles.title: Occasional Reviewers
Reconceptualizing Parent‐Adolescent Relationships: A Dialogic Model
articles.abstract: The author applies a dialogic view of communication to parent‐adolescent relationships, allowing for explicit attention to the process of interaction and social construction of meaning within these relationships. The constitutive role of dialogue between parent and adolescent is set within the context of competing tensions or dialectics. This theoretical framework provides a perspective for attending to parents' and adolescents' experiences and relational interactions, as well as meaning making and identity formation occurring within the dialogic gap.

articles.title: Religion and Family Links: Neofunctionalist Reflections ‐ by Donald Swenson
Skilled Support Within Intimate Relationships
articles.authors: Rafaeli, Eshkol; Gleason, Marci E. J.
articles.abstract: The literature on social support within dyadic intimate relationships raises a seeming paradox: The availability of support tends to reduce distress, but its actual receipt is often unhelpful and at times engenders feelings of inadequacy, indebtedness, and inequity—unintended but potent side effects of the support transaction. Our review organizes this literature in order to solve the apparent paradox. Specifically, we theorize that, because support attempts are often unskilled and miscarried, they lead to greater costs than benefits. We identify four ways in which dyadic support can be unskillful, ways pertaining to its timing, content, process, or reciprocation. We suggest that when these are addressed, support can regain its intended goals of enhancing dyadic coping, reducing stress, and strengthening relationships.

Theorizing Lesbian and Gay Parenting: Past, Present, and Future Scholarship
articles.abstract: Research on lesbian and gay parenting has stimulated theoretical advancement in family studies. Subjective understandings of lesbian and gay parents offer scholars a novel lens through which to view identity construction, management, and negotiation. Triggered by a recent queer shift in family research, however, some lesbian and gay parenting scholarship has begun to critique identity theories as constructing hegemony around the identity “gay” or “lesbian” in that they assume a uniform subject. Queer theory challenges the foundations of identity scholarship; unpacks the assumptions that underlie research on families, gender, and sexualities; and deconstructs how the rubric of difference has framed and limited existing knowledge. I conclude with suggestions for complicating and expanding queer theory.

articles.title: Triangles: Bowen Family Systems Theory Perspectives. Peter Titelman (Ed.).
Uses and Misuses of Bronfenbrenner's Bioecological Theory of Human Development
articles.authors: Tudge, Jonathan R. H.; Mokrova, Irina; Hatfield, Bridget E.; Karnik, Rachana B.
articles.abstract: This paper evaluates the application of Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory as it is represented in empirical work on families and their relationships. We describe the “mature” form of bioecological theory of the mid‐1990s and beyond, with its focus on proximal processes at the center of the Process‐Person‐Context‐Time model. We then examine 25 papers published since 2001, all explicitly described as being based on Bronfenbrenner's theory, and show that all but 4 rely on outmoded versions of the theory, resulting in conceptual confusion and inadequate testing of the theory.
